implementation_notes: The standard library provides the pattern as threading.local: each thread that touches the object sees its own attribute dictionary, and the documented way to give every thread a fresh value is to subclass local and define __init__, which is called once per thread. The classic key/collection/proxy structure disappears into the object - no key is allocated, no lookup is written - and values persist for the thread's lifetime, since there is no thread-exit destructor hook, so cleanup belongs to the work item. threading.local is correct only while the work item is the thread; asyncio tasks share one thread, which is why the contextvars documentation states that context managers with state should use Context Variables instead.
pitfalls: A threading.local is shared by every asyncio task running on one thread, so an async handler that stores state there leaks it to concurrent tasks - use contextvars.ContextVar in async code.
There is no per-thread cleanup hook: values live until the thread dies or the attribute is deleted, so pooled workers keep the last work item's objects alive.
Subclassing local and defining __slots__ defeats thread-local storage - the documentation notes that slots are shared across threads; keep per-thread state in __dict__ attributes.
New threads start with an empty local (nothing is inherited), and in free-threaded builds the thread context copied at start depends on sys.flags.thread_inherit_context.

variants.name: contextvars.ContextVar (context-local state)
variants.implementation_notes: contextvars.ContextVar binds the value to the current context rather than to the current thread: it is created once at module level, set() returns a Token that reset() uses to restore the previous value, and each asyncio task runs in its own copied context, so two concurrent requests never see each other's value (PEP 567, standard since Python 3.7). It works in threads too - every thread has its own context stack - which makes it the single primitive for both synchronous and asynchronous code. Use it for request-scoped values that are read far away from where they are set; it replaces threading.local in the classic context-manager idiom the standard library documents.
variants.code_sketch:
import contextvars

current: contextvars.ContextVar[RequestContext] = contextvars.ContextVar("current")

async def handle(request):
    token = current.set(RequestContext(request))   # bound to this task's context
    try:
        await service.invoke(request)
    finally:
        current.reset(token)                       # restores the previous value
pitfalls: ContextVars must be created at module top level, never in closures: Context objects hold strong references to variables and prevent them from being garbage collected.
A set() inside a task is local to that task's context copy - the caller does not see it unless the value or the token is returned explicitly.

reset() must be called with the matching token, in reverse order; a leaked token leaves a value bound for the rest of the context's life, and a Context.run() recursion or cross-thread use raises RuntimeError.
